item.title: OpenAI discloses four more rogue incidents (101 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://fortune.com/2026/10/16/openai-discloses-four-more-rogue-incidents-involving-financial-medical-and-government-data/, See on Hacker News

OpenAI has added four more cases of misbehaving AI agents to a disclosures page it stood up following the Hugging Face hack in July, in an effort to be more transparent.

The incidents OpenAI disclosed this week all occurred in June, but OpenAI was not aware of three of them until months later in August or September.

Of the 19 total incidents OpenAI details on the disclosure page, most occurred in May or June, but OpenAI did not discover or disclose them until months later. The earliest incident is from January, and the most recent is from Oct. 6.

All of the incidents are examples of what AI researchers call “misalignment,” which is when an AI model fails to follow instructions or takes actions that the person developing the model did not authorize and would not have wanted the model to take. There is no known, silver-bullet solution to preventing this behavior, and it is an active area of research.

Downloading 24 years of unauthorized hospital bed data

Of the four cases OpenAI uploaded this week, it marked two as “critical.” In one of the critical cases, an internal model that was “highly persistent” downloaded 24 years of hospital bed data from an unnamed government website without permission. OpenAI did not immediately respond to Fortune’s request for comment on which government website it was.

The website initially blocked the agent’s request, but the AI ultimately found a way to bypass the access controls. Multiple times along the way, the agent’s “chain of thought,” in which an agent writes down its reasoning steps, indicated that the model itself was questioning if its actions were “ethical,” but it ultimately proceeded.

On OpenAI’s side, another AI model that acted as an automated grader of the research task the other AI model was trying to fulfill did not consistently flag this behavior as problematic. It “marked some responses incorrect and others correct,” the report said. The way graders assess AI behavior can shape whether it occurs again. In a Sept. 11 essay on misalignment by Turing Award–winner Yoshua Bengio, he said the Hugging Face incident may have occurred because automated graders rewarded cheating and hacking in previous training runs.

“With the OpenAI agents, there is reason to believe successful cheating was actually rewarded: When the scoring program does not see the cheating, it pays out anyway, and such cheats become more likely next time,” Bengio said.

OpenAI says it has since improved its security as well as its alignment grading. “In response to this and to other incidents, we’ve strengthened our security controls, blocked models from accessing the live internet during training or evaluation, improved our alignment grading, and extended our misalignment monitoring to all reinforcement learning and evaluation traffic,” the company noted.

The most recent incident OpenAI has disclosed, which occurred on Oct. 6, involved one of the AI models the company uses as an automated grader. In that case, the grader tried to upload fraudulent reports on what it had found in an evaluation. This is an example of why relying on AI models to grade the training runs of other AI models can be problematic.

Making an unauthorized purchase with someone else’s cryptocurrency

In another disclosed case, a model in the GPT-5.6 Sol family—the predecessor to OpenAI’s current flagship model, GPT-6 Astra—accessed a cryptocurrency wallet the human testers had not provided it, and made an unauthorized payment to complete a task during testing. This occurred on June 26. OpenAI discovered it in September.

“The model questioned whether it had permission” to make the purchase, OpenAI said, again referring to what the model had recorded about its own reasoning in its chain of thought. It then reasoned with itself that since it found the information publicly, it could use it. In the model’s chain-of-thought logs, it figured that since the wallet it found was public, that “funds could be stolen anytime.”

It then concluded, “We can deploy!” It later asked itself again if the act was done “ethically,” and reasoned that the funds were “effectively abandoned.”

Getting internet access, changing live systems

The other incident OpenAI flagged as critical involved a model looking up public data, which theoretically is acceptable, but in the process it accessed the organization’s internal system, made changes to it, and was still able to “retain access … even after reverting the changes,” OpenAI said. It also downloaded 147,451 rows from nonpublic data tables. Perhaps most concerningly, the model did not disclose any of its actions to the evaluators.

In the final case OpenAI disclosed, an AI agent was able to get internet access from a research environment that should have been isolated—potentially similar to what happened during the Hugging Face incident, in which hundreds of AI agents were able to get internet access, although OpenAI did not directly compare these two incidents.

In the newly disclosed case, the agent knew it was not allowed to access the web, so it asked “external services” to perform actions it was blocked from doing. It did this even after it had found another way to answer the question, and also continued to develop its crafty work-around even after completing the task.

item.title: GLP-1 may slow biological aging (143 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://www.universityofcalifornia.edu/news/new-study-shows-popular-glp-1-weight-loss-drug-may-slow-biological-aging, See on Hacker News

Semaglutide, a widely used weight loss drug sometimes sold as Ozempic or Wegovy, slowed biological aging across multiple epigenetic clocks in a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled clinical trial.

Credit: iStock/Eduardo Monroy Husillos

Beyond the widespread attention GLP-1 drugs are receiving for treating obesity, lowering blood sugar and decreasing the risk of cardiovascular disease, emerging research is investigating their other potential impacts — including their effects on aging.

Now, a new study provides the first randomized, placebo-controlled clinical evidence that semaglutide, a widely used GLP-1 drug, slows down the accumulation of biological aging markers in the DNA of adults with HIV. The study is published in Nature Communications.

Researchers at the University of California, San Diego and several partner institutions analyzed data from a previously published clinical trial of 108 adults with HIV‑associated lipohypertrophy, a condition in which excess fat builds up around the abdomen. About half of the participants received weekly injections of semaglutide, with the rest receiving placebo injections.

The team used a set of biological “epigenetic clocks” to track cellular aging over the 32-week treatment period. These clocks detect DNA methylation, chemical marks on DNA that help regulate how genes are turned on or off without changing the genetic sequence itself. By measuring changes in these marks, the team could assess whether the treatment was associated with a slower or faster biological aging pattern.

People with HIV often experience accelerated aging, even if it is well-controlled with antiretroviral therapy, according to first author Michael Corley, Ph.D., associate professor at UC San Diego School of Medicine and the Stein Institute for Research on Aging. However, the study found compared to the placebo group:

  • Participants treated with semaglutide exhibited a broad pattern of slower biological aging across epigenetic clocks linked to inflammation and blood, brain, heart, kidney, liver and metabolic health.

  • The drug slowed the pace of biological aging by 9 %, as measured by the DunedinPACE epigenetic clock.

  • The drug significantly slowed biological processes associated with the risk of all‑cause mortality and age-related disease, as measured by the PCGrimAge epigenetic clock.

Research suggests there are several mechanisms by which semaglutide may influence biological aging. By reducing inflammation and metabolic stress, GLP-1 drugs decreased chronic immune activation, a primary driver of accelerated aging in people with HIV. They also reduce visceral and ectopic fat that accumulates around the abdomen and organs, which may help curb the inflammatory and metabolic signals that promote aging.

“Emerging data also suggest that GLP-1 drugs may reprogram certain cells in different organs, which could help explain why we see effects across multiple aging clocks,” said Corley.

While the study focused on people with HIV‑associated lipohypertrophy, Corley says it may also offer lessons for the wider population.

“Many of the biological processes we study in HIV are also central to aging in the general population,” he said. “Because these processes can emerge earlier or be more pronounced in people with HIV, this community can help us identify interventions that may improve healthspan more broadly.”

We are not saying that semaglutide reverses aging or makes people younger. What we are seeing is a signal that it may slow some of the biological processes associated with aging.

Michael Corley, Ph.D.

In a related pilot study published in npj Aging last month, Corley and another team of researchers found that taking semaglutide for 24 weeks:

  • Reduced the rate of biological aging for 42% of participants with HIV and metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) — also known as fatty liver disease — as measured by the DunedinPACE epigenetic clock. Those participants also had a greater reduction in liver fat compared with participants whose pace of aging sped up.

  • Slowed aging associated with the risk of all‑cause mortality in 34% of participants as measured by the PCGrimAge epigenetic clock.

  • Increased the length of telomeres — repetitive DNA sequences at the ends of chromosomes that protect genetic material — in nearly 49 % of participants as measured by the PCDNAmTL epigenetic clock. Those participants also tended to walk faster after treatment, suggesting better physical function.

Together, these studies add to growing evidence that GLP-1 drugs may influence pathways involved in biological aging.

“We are not saying that semaglutide reverses aging or makes people younger,” said Corley. “What we are seeing is a signal that it may slow some of the biological processes associated with aging. With newer GLP-1–based therapies now emerging, the field has an opportunity to test whether different drugs in this class have distinct effects on aging biology and to identify which patients may benefit most.”

Larger clinical trials are needed to confirm the findings, determine how long treatment effects last, and establish optimal dosing and treatment duration for both people with HIV and the broader population. Future studies will also be needed to test whether the effects of GLP-1 effects on aging biology are enhanced when combined with lifestyle interventions such as diet, exercise and sleep optimization.

The Stein Institute for Research on Aging plans to translate these results into individualized “aging dashboards” to track biological aging with epigenetic clocks, enabling clinicians to design personalized therapies that target the underlying mechanisms of aging and help prevent age‑related diseases.

Additional co-authors on the Nature Communications study include: Alina P. S. Pang at UC San Diego;  Varun Dwaraka and Ryan Smith at TruDiagnostic; Danielle Labbato and Grace A. McComsey at University Hospitals Cleveland Medical Center; Allison Ross Eckard at the Medical University of South Carolina; and Grace A. McComsey at Case Western Reserve University. The study was funded, in part, by the National Institutes of Health (grants P30 AI036214, R01DK121619 and UM1TR004528) and the James B. Pendleton Charitable Trust.

Additional co-authors on the npj Aging study include: Alina P. S. Pang at UC San Diego; Douglas W. Kitch and Amy Kantor at Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health; Fred Sattler at University of Southern California Keck School of Medicine; Pablo F. Belaunzaran‑Zamudio at the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases. Todd T. Brown at Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine; Alan Landay at the University of Texas Medical Branch; Jordan E. Lake at UTHealth Houston; and Kristine M. Erlandson at University of Colorado Anschutz Medical Campus. The study was funded, in part, by the National Institutes of Health (grants P30 AI036214, UM1 AI068634, UM1 AI068636, UM1 AI106701) and the James B. Pendleton Charitable Trust.

Corley serves as a scientific advisor for TruDiagnostic.

item.title: Amazon uses AI to monitor union risk in UK warehouses (121 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://www.opendemocracy.net/amazon-ai-surveillance-monitor-union-activity-uk-warehouses-birmingham-coventry-atlas-sutton-coldfield/, See on Hacker News

Garfield Hylton has long known that Amazon monitors and logs every minute of his working day. Every product he scans, every second he takes between scans, every time his scanner is briefly inactive – all of it is tracked, recorded, and used to set productivity targets and predictions. 

But what 62-year-old Hylton didn’t know is that Amazon seemingly also monitors potential “dissent” in the Coventry warehouse where he works, using AI to surveil posts on social media and the company’s internal staff bulletin board.

Internal documents made public as part of a court battle between Amazon and a Canadian union suggest the tech giant uses Atlas, an in-house AI forecasting tool, to predict how likely its warehouse staff in the US, Canada and the UK are to attempt to form a union, stage a sit-in, or conduct other “disruptive labour events”.

The documents, which appear to be training resources for Amazon managers in Canada, contain an appendix stating Atlas amasses “hundreds of data points” – including posts on Reddit forums and employees’ responses to internal feedback surveys, as well as wider information on the workplace and any previous industrial action – to award warehouses a risk score of between 100 and 900 for union activity.

The lower the score, the more likely Atlas believes workers – whom Amazon calls ‘associates’ – in that warehouse are to unionise or take other actions that could impact Amazon’s productivity or profitability. The document states that for the company’s leadership, higher scores are “better”.

This “makes it clear that they think the union is bad”, Michael Newman, a partner at London-based law firm Leigh Day, told openDemocracy. Newman said it tells “a very different story” from Amazon’s previous assertions that it does not seek to prevent workers from joining a union.

Warehouses appear to be categorised into five tiers based on their Atlas score, where Tier 5 is “no immediate perceived risk” and Tier 1 is “future activity is imminent”. The document suggests this scale can be used to “inform staffing decisions, resource planning, standard actions, and ownership to mitigate risks to Amazon labour structure”.

An Amazon spokesperson refuted the characterisation of Atlas as “individual employee monitoring or surveillance”, stating: “This is site/building level activity only.” 

They added that the company does “not track individual employees’ opinions, affiliations or union membership”, or any “personal data”, and said Atlas is not used to monitor dissent, but to “help us understand where associates need more support and to ensure we’re addressing issues that they raise”.

In total, 16 Amazon warehouses across the US, Canada and the UK are “Tier 1”, according to the document. Two are in the UK: a £500m robotic-fulfilment centre in Sutton Coldfield, north-east Birmingham (referred to by Amazon as EMA4), and the warehouse where Hylton works near Coventry (BHX4).

Hylton, whose role involves receiving goods into the warehouse and dispatching them on to other warehouses, is a member of the GMB union. He believes the extent of the data Amazon has collected on his colleagues creates a huge power imbalance, with workers having only their own experiences to defend themselves.

“It’s not right in a democracy… the employer should not be interfering,” he said, speaking to openDemocracy soon after learning about the Atlas tool from GMB. “Workers should be allowed to decide if they wish to choose to unionise,” he continued, adding: “If you're then monitoring, you're undermining a process deliberately and willfully.”

Rachel Fagan, an organiser for GMB, told openDemocracy: “It’s quite clear from these documents that these sites are being monitored for union activity. Everyone knows that Amazon is heavy on surveillance, but this becomes more personal.

“Amazon is using this technology to essentially outwit or manoeuvre workers that want to organise [a union]. Nothing in this fight against Amazon is an even playing field; they have all the wealth, all the technology, everything to their disposal and they use it,” she added. 

GMB has long tried to unionise Amazon workers in the UK, coming closest to winning formal recognition in Coventry in July 2024. Employees at the warehouse became the first in the country to take strike action against Amazon in January 2023, and around 2,600 took part in an official ballot for union recognition at the site six months later, which GMB lost by just 28 votes. 

The union and Foxglove, a tech justice non-profit, have accused Amazon of using “dirty tricks” to swing the vote in its favour. These include the mass hiring of non-unionised workers and allegedly plastering QR codes that employees could scan to cancel their GMB membership over screens, cafeteria tables, and toilet doors in the warehouse in the run-up to the vote.

Foxglove and Leigh Day are representing two workers in a legal challenge against Amazon’s use of ‘click-to-quit’ QR codes. They argue that the tool was an attempt to “bully” workers into ending their union membership.

The documents revealing Amazon’s Atlas AI tool were disclosed as part of a legal challenge by Canadian union Unifor and shared with US non-profit publication Truthout. The British Columbia Labour Board ultimately ruled that Amazon had violated multiple local labour laws, following an earlier ruling that found the company had unlawfully imposed a wage freeze on unionised workers at a warehouse outside Vancouver.

Rosa Curling, co-executive director of Foxglove, described the level of surveillance detailed in the document as “highly intrusive”, showing that Amazon has a “very intentional policy to try and bust organising, bust unionising efforts, and they are using all sorts of tools to do that”.

Curling continued: “We are actively reviewing these documents to see what additional arguments, if any, we should be adding to our existing claim to unlawful inducement, or indeed on like this ongoing breach of workers' rights to organise, which is a well-respected right in UK-made laws.”

Amazon told openDemocracy that a framework called Atlas is not currently used in the UK. The company had not responded to our question about whether it uses a similar system with a different name at the time of publishing.

Commenting on the AI system, Leigh Day’s Newman added: “Now we know Atlas is used by Amazon, we’ll be asking more questions about what data points are used, how these scores were reached.” 

Amazon has previously been found guilty of “excessive” surveillance of its workers. In 2022, French data watchdog CNIL fined the company €32m (£27m) for breaching General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) rules by tracking worker activity so precisely that an alert was triggered if workers were inactive for between one and 10 minutes.

Asked whether Amazon’s Atlas tool is an appropriate level of worker surveillance, a government spokesperson said: “Employers and workers have a shared interest in workplace monitoring technologies being used transparently and in ways that are fair, accountable and reliable, so that they can support productivity and good management while maintaining trust in the workplace. 

“We expect all employers to respect workers’ rights to take part in lawful trade union activity.” 

An Amazon spokesperson said: “The GMB's characterisation is wrong. This isn’t surveillance. Like any responsible employer, we have numerous ways for our team to provide us with feedback, and we use that feedback to identify where we can improve the day-to-day experience of our employees.

“Our employees always have the choice of whether or not to join a union. What matters most to us is the direct relationship between our teams and their managers – it means every person’s voice is heard, not just a few, and that when someone spots a way to improve their job, we can act on it quickly. We’ve made real progress in recent years on the things that matter, like pay and safety, and we know there’s always more to do. That’s our focus: getting better every day.”

item.title: US federal budget deficit jumps 12% in one year to nearly $2 Trillion (144 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://finance.yahoo.com/economy/policy/article/the-us-federal-budget-deficit-for-2026-just-came-in-its-1992-trillion-191917669.html, See on Hacker News

The US federal budget deficit for 2026 officially came in Friday at $1.992 trillion, a final tabulation to close out the government's fiscal year and another reminder of Washington's spiraling reliance on red ink.

This deficit number represents about 6% of the US gross domestic product and was a result of $5.403 trillion in total revenues for the fiscal year against total spending of $7.396 trillion.

The 2026 reading is a 12% jump from 2025's $1.775 trillion deficit.

These final numbers came in the Treasury Department's Monthly Statement for September, which covers the final month in the US government's fiscal calendar.

The red ink has led to dire warnings from economists that the US now routinely runs annual deficits that were previously seen only during recessions and wars. The gross US national debt passed $40 trillion in August and now sits above $40.3 trillion.

The latest "Debt to the Penny" reading from the Treasury Department came this past Wednesday, putting the gross US national debt at $40,329,229,827,541.02.

Read more: How the soaring federal debt affects you personally

The independent budget hawks at the Committee for a Responsible Budget noted in a recent analysis that "the country's future fiscal outlook is even more dismal," noting that annual deficits could reach $3.1 trillion by 2036 without a change in the fiscal trajectory.

The group noted that annual interest costs on the debt are now $1.1 trillion, a record 3.4% of GDP, making it the second-largest line item in the government's budget. Interest on the debt still costs less than Social Security, but it is now more expensive than either Medicare or the defense budget.

Members of President Trump's team have tried to downplay this year's tabulation — the highest annual deficit reading other than 2020 and 2021, when budgets were inflated by COVID-era spending — as a blip and insist that the US fiscal situation is getting under control.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has focused on the Supreme Court-ordered tariff refunds that have turned a revenue stream into a cost center for the government in recent months.

Indeed, the impact of tariff refunds has been significant: $144.6 billion in tariff refunds were given out over the past year — but analyses of the deficit also show a variety of factors that have driven up deficits.

A Hamilton Project tracker of government expenditures shows how government spending has increased at a steady pace in 2026. The tracker looks at spending by calendar year and shows that as of Oct. 14, government spending has jumped each of the last three years.

item.title: Solar surpasses nuclear power globally for first time – pv magazine Global (353 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://www.pv-magazine.com/2026/09/29/solar-surpasses-nuclear-power-globally-for-first-time/, See on Hacker News

Solar and wind are increasingly outpacing nuclear power globally, with solar generation surpassing nuclear for the first time in 2025, according to WNISR 2026. The report highlights nuclear’s slow growth, lengthy construction timelines and limited small modular reactor deployment, contrasting them with rapid renewables and battery expansion.

The World Nuclear Industry Status Report (WNISR) 2026, overseen by French nuclear energy consultant Mycle Schneider, shows that wind power alone surpassed nuclear generation on a monthly basis in March 2025, followed by solar in April – the first time global monthly solar generation exceeded nuclear output.

From March 2025 through June 2026, either solar or wind individually generated more electricity than nuclear every month. In March, April and May 2026, both technologies independently surpassed nuclear generation.

Increasing gap

According to the report, the gap between renewables and nuclear widened substantially in 2025. Global solar capacity increased by 510 GW to 2,383 GW, up 27% year on year, while wind added a record 159 GW to reach 1,291 GW, an increase of 14%. By comparison, installed nuclear capacity rose by just 1.5 GW to 399.5 GW, while operating nuclear capacity declined by 0.5 GW to 368.6 GW. The report notes that nuclear capacity has remained essentially flat for more than 25 years, while wind and, particularly, solar have expanded rapidly.

The report’s PV figures, however, are based on relatively conservative estimates. More recent data from IEA PVPS indicate that global PV additions reached around 690 GW in 2025, about 180 GW more than the figure used by WNISR. This suggests the gap between solar and nuclear capacity – and their respective growth rates – was even wider than indicated in the report.

“The reality of the nuclear industry on the ground is quite sobering for those who expected to find a booming sector,” Schneider told pv magazine. “Recently, U.S. nuclear company Holtec put an initial public offering (IPO) on hold just days before its planned stock market listing, through which it had hoped to raise almost $1 billion. Its peer, Fermi, has lost about 80% of its stock value since it was first listed in October 2025.”

“The main reason? These companies have little or nothing to show on the ground to convince investors to continue providing cash,” he added. “Meanwhile, the world’s operating nuclear fleet increased output by 1.1% – with output declining outside China – while global solar power generation jumped by a stunning 30%, surpassing nuclear’s annual electricity production for the first time. One is tempted to say: It’s the growth rates, stupid!”

The report identifies falling battery costs as a potential enabler of continued PV expansion, particularly as grids contend with growing volumes of variable renewable generation and periods of low or negative electricity prices. Grid-scale battery deployment accelerated sharply in 2025, with 104 GW and 257 GWh connected during the year. More than 78% of cumulative battery energy storage system (BESS) capacity was installed between 2023 and 2025.

Slow expansion

The report shows that the global nuclear sector is expanding slowly, with most new activity concentrated in China and Russia. As of July 1, 2026, 411 reactors were operating in 31 countries, excluding 30 units in long-term outage, with operating capacity at 374.7 GW. In 2025, nuclear plants generated 2,703 TWh, up 1.1% year on year, largely driven by a 7.6% increase in China. Outside China, nuclear generation declined by 0.2% and remained well below its 2006 level. Nuclear’s share of global electricity generation slipped to 8.8%, its lowest level in four and a half decades and roughly half its 1996 peak of 17.5%.

Four reactors started supplying electricity in 2025, while seven closed, resulting in the first negative annual reactor balance since 2021. Between 2006 and 2025, 104 reactors started up and 106 closed. China accounted for 53 of those startups and no closures, meaning the rest of the world recorded a net decline of 55 reactors. Although global nuclear capacity increased by a net 21.5 GW over the two decades, China alone added 52.3 GW, while capacity outside the country fell by almost 30.7 GW.

The construction pipeline has nevertheless expanded. Seventy-three reactors were under construction as of July 1, the highest number since 1987, with China accounting for 37. Russia remains the dominant international supplier, with Russian technology involved in 29 reactors under construction worldwide, including 22 outside Russia. Nine out of 10 reactors being built are in Asia or Eastern Europe.

Long construction times and delays remain a feature of new nuclear projects, according to the report. None of the 16 reactors connected to the grid between 2023 and 2025 was completed on schedule, with an average construction period of 10.9 years. Of 13 reactors scheduled to start generating electricity in 2025, only four did so. Some projects have experienced exceptionally long timelines, including Slovakia’s Mochovce-4, where construction began more than 40 years ago, and Iran’s Bushehr-2, where construction originally started in 1976.

Construction starts accelerated in 2025, however, reaching 12 units, the highest annual total since 2010. Nine were in China, two in Russia and one in South Korea. Of the 52 reactor construction starts recorded worldwide between 2020 and 2025, all but one involved the Chinese or Russian nuclear industries, either domestically or abroad.

Limited progress on small modular reactors

The report questions whether small modular reactors (SMRs) can deliver on their long-standing commercial promises, noting that progress remains limited despite growing government support and public funding.

“For decades, small modular reactors have been held out as holding great promise for expanding nuclear power into various new markets. Remarkably similar claims have been made by the nuclear industry in multiple countries. Nowhere have these claims come true,” the authors said.

The authors challenge several claimed advantages of SMRs, including lower costs, modular construction, improved safety, reduced waste and easier siting. Many commercially proposed designs are 300 MW or larger, while an analysis cited in the report suggests some SMR designs could generate between two and 30 times more nuclear waste than larger reactors.

The report also questions whether modular manufacturing can achieve economies of scale without a large and predictable market. Still, SMR projects are advancing in several countries. Canada began construction of GE-Hitachi’s BWRX-300 in 2026, while China continued testing its Linglong One demonstration reactor. Russia is developing floating and land-based SMRs, while the Czech Republic and Sweden are pursuing Rolls-Royce projects. The report questions whether the EU can meet its goal of deploying its first SMRs by the early 2030s.

The United Kingdom has committed £2.6 billion ($3.5 billion) to advance three Rolls-Royce reactors at Wylfa, with a final investment decision expected in 2029. At 470 MW, the design exceeds the commonly used 300 MW threshold for SMRs.

In the United States, federal funding supports projects involving GE Vernova, TerraPower, X-energy and Kairos Power. While some have reached permitting or construction stages, many remain years from commercial operation. Overall, the report says SMR development remains heavily dependent on public funding, while commercial deployment, construction timelines and the claimed benefits of modular construction remain uncertain.

Global overview

The report also provides detailed country-level assessments covering developments in major nuclear markets and potential newcomer countries, as well as nuclear decommissioning, the Fukushima disaster and Russia’s nuclear interdependencies.

These sections examine reactor operations, newbuild plans, closures, policy developments and the challenges associated with aging fleets. The report also tracks the dismantling of closed reactors, developments in Japan 15 years after the Fukushima accident, and the nuclear industry’s continuing technology, fuel and supply-chain links with Russia.

item.title: Making Chicken Transparent Using Dorito Dust (187 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://chillphysicsenjoyer.substack.com/p/making-chicken-transparent-using, See on Hacker News

Thank you Adaobi for such a wonderful suggestion. All credit to her for the idea, we are still workin’ on it!

My genius friend Adaobi Adibe sent me a paper on making biological tissues transparent. In “Achieving optical transparency in live animals with absorbing molecules”, the authors make biological tissues, like chicken breast, transparent by soaking them in a solution of tartrazine. Tartrazine is the very bright yellowish-orange food dye that is found on Doritos.

We aim to do a more ambitious replication imminently. But as a warm up, I tried to replicate parts of this protocol by soaking chicken breast in tartrazine solution. I got partial transparency but not to the degree of the paper. The sample below is an approximately 2mm thick raw chicken breast cut from a 5mm slice that was soaked in ~0.19 M tartrazine solution for 6 hours at room temperature. I took an image of this with a desk light. You can see the grid lines showing through from underneath. The chicken, even though the texture to the touch is the same, has a visual quality like that of gummy bears.

The original paper used 0.62 M, 40 °C and a machine shaker, but I couldn't find a way to do this safely, nor did I have the equipment to do so. Hence the altered protocol.

The image below is a different angle of my sample. The sample on the left is the same 2mm thick chicken breast slice as above. And the sample on the right is a control where I soaked it in water (it is slightly yellow since this process is super messy and I got dust on it).

In the top part of the sample we do see some transparency, with the 5mm x 5mm grid showing through. The visual quality of the chicken breast takes on a gummy-bear like quality. Kinda makes me wanna chew it if it wouldn't give me Salmonella.

I don't wanna get copyrighted by Doritos so here is a cartoon of where you can find tartrazine in the wild.

How does this work?

The current model we have is that the absorbance properties of the tartrazine also shift the refractive index of water. By pushing the refractive index of water to that of protein and lipid solution, we make the object more transparent. I’ll explain this in great detail later.

Tartrazine was from APC Pure. It was >80% dye content, which means some uncertainty over what the true molar concentration will be. I then prepared three concentrations of tartrazine at these molar concentrations, one of which was just a 0 concentration as a control.

  • Tartrazine: 0 g, Tap water: 20 g, w/w: 0%, Molality (mol/kg water): 0, Tartrazine (mmol): 0, Molarity (approx.): 0 M (control)

  • Tartrazine: 2 g, Tap water: 18 g, w/w: 10%, Molality (mol/kg water): 0.21, Tartrazine (mmol): 3.7, Molarity (approx.): ~0.19 M

  • Tartrazine: 6 g, Tap water: 14 g, w/w: 30%, Molality (mol/kg water): 0.80, Tartrazine (mmol): 11.2, Molarity (approx.): ~0.56 M

Tartrazine has M = 534.4 g/mol. Moles use the nominal mass (the powder is >80% dye, so true values are up to ~15% lower). Molarity assumes a final solution volume of ~20 mL.

This is what the tartrazine looked like. It doesn't have an odour, and it seems to be considered food safe by the FDA, so I didn't bother wearing gloves for this bit. Here is a picture of the tartrazine and the specs.

  • Product: Tartrazine E102 FG, C.I. 19140

  • Dye content: >80%

  • Molecular formula: C16H9N4Na3O9S2

  • Molecular weight: 534.37 g/mol

  • λmax (in water): 425 nm

  • Water-insoluble matter: <0.20%

  • Subsidiary dyes: <1.00%

  • Heavy metals (as Pb): <40 mg/kg

To prepare the solutions I used a jeweller's scale to weigh out the right amounts and then added tap water to the weights listed in the table.

To dissolve the tartrazine, I mixed it with a glass stirrer at room temperature until there were no visible lumps.¹

Here are the different solutions at different concentrations, the most concentrated one on the left, the middle concentration in the middle, and then a water control on the right.

Next, I got chicken breast fillets from Tesco. I cut a 5mm thick slab and then cut three pieces out to around 15mm in length.

I then soaked 5mm thick slices of chicken breast in each of the three solutions.

After 6 hours of soaking, these were the results.

First, the chicken in the highest concentration solution failed, because the tartrazine seemed to crystallise. This is what it looked like - it got all crusty.

For the middle concentration (~0.19 M), the chicken appeared gelatinous. But it wasn't transparent. The control chicken remained completely opaque.

I threw these pieces out and then tried again with the method below.

And then I tried again with the same procedure, with the aim of soaking it for 12 hours at room temperature. Given the issues with the highest concentration (~0.56 M), I only tried the water control and the middle concentration (~0.19 M). But this time I put the chicken in test tubes and covered it, given that I was gonna leave it out for 12 hours at room temperature. I wanted to mitigate the food safety risk.

This was the 12-hour-soaked piece. Whilst it's hard to see with the camera, there was some slight visible translucency compared to the control.

To examine it I put it under some light above.

I then cut approximately 2mm slices of chicken. This was quite fiddly to do with a small slimy piece. Here is what it looked like compared to the control.

This technique has been used to make fluorescence imaging much easier in live animals.

On my end, doing this well could add to the set of things that independent scientists could image at home. We might be able to probe internal structures of things more casually. Making things transparent would give better images and would allow independent scientists to look at tissue structure more closely.

Effective observation at low cost is one of the themes of my research. I wrote about writing tracing software for Brownian particles using my microscope in my last post. I am also thinking about trying to match the performance of CO2 gas sensing using pressure, which would make that type of sensing cheaper. In line with this theme, I’m super excited about attempting weird and cool techniques to make structures more easier to probe!

Here’s is more than you ever wanted to know about optical transparency.

A material can be opaque for two reasons. First, a material can absorb light and block it. Second, it can scramble light due to different refractive indices.

First, light rays from the other side could be absorbed when they pass through. If light is absorbed, the light can't hit your eyes and you can't see the other side. Light can have multiple wavelengths, and the wavelengths absorbed by the material are determined by the material's spectra. To calculate the spectra, we can approximate the physical behaviour of molecules to that of an electron around a potential. The Schrödinger equation tells us that this system can only occupy a discrete set of energies, and it tells us which ones these are. The differences between these energies set the wavelengths that are ultimately absorbed by the material.

In reality, materials are composed of lots of different things and so we expect them to also absorb different wavelengths.

Another reason for opacity is less obvious, but more interesting. The refractive index of a material tells us how quickly light travels within the medium. When light travels between materials with different refractive indices, it deflects slightly. When a material is packed with sub-materials that have different refractive indices, the refraction within causes light rays to get scattered since light rays ping around.

Biological materials contain a mix of different sub-materials inside - fibres, cells, proteins, and more. Each of these materials contains a different refractive index. When you have a material with one refractive index embedded in a material with a different refractive index, you get scattering. This scattering causes the light from the other side to get scrambled. The diagram below shows this.

We can model biological materials as a 'base material' of water, with chunks of lipids and proteins embedded inside, all of which have different refractive indices.

To make something transparent, we need to exploit the two causes of opacity. One approach is to try to change the absorbance spectra of a material so that it absorbs fewer wavelengths of light.

Alternatively (and this is the approach we'll cover in this post), we could try to change the refractive index of the water inside to match the embedded media. The image below shows this principle with biological tissues. If you can change the refractive index of water with a dye, you can then match it to the refractive index of proteins and lipids, which is slightly higher.

If you manage to do this without modifying the absorbance of a material, you should be able to make it more transparent.

Ok, so the game is to change the refractive index. Here is a map of the calculations we need to do to figure out how to modify the refractive index of a material.

To understand where the refractive index plays a part in a quantitative model, let's model how light travels according to Maxwell. Light is an electromagnetic wave, comprised of oscillating electric and magnetic waves. For this essay, let's focus on the electric field part to get the key intuitions.

Using complex representation, if light travels down the z axis, in a vacuum, we can write down the equation of light as the following. Because it's a wave, we can write

\(E(z, t) = E_0 \cos\!\left(\frac{\omega z}{c} - \omega t\right)\)

But for convenience we use complex numbers

\(E(z, t) = \mathrm{Re}\left\{ E_0\, e^{\,i\omega z / c \;-\; i\omega t} \right\}\)

Where E₀ is the amplitude (how strong the field is), ω is the angular frequency (at a fixed point the field goes round once every T = 2π/ω), c is the speed of light, z is distance along the beam and t is time. Crest to crest, the wavelength is λ = 2πc/ω.

In media though, we expect both the speed of light to change in the medium, as well as some absorption. We can rewrite the equation as follows

\(E(z, t) = \mathrm{Re}\left\{ E_0\, e^{\,i(n' + i\kappa)\,\omega z / c \;-\; i\omega t} \right\} = \mathrm{Re}\left\{ E_0\, e^{-\kappa \omega z / c}\, e^{\,i(n' \omega z / c \;-\; \omega t)} \right\}\)

The coefficient in the exponential n′ is a multiplier behind the spatial term, and represents the real refractive index. κ represents how much the wave attenuates, and is meant to denote absorption.

In practice we can group n′ + iκ as one number, and then refer to this as the complex refractive index.

First we need to try to change the real refractive index. If we can increase the refractive index of water to match the tissue refractive index, we would have a more transparent material. Water has a refractive index of 1.33. And although this number is variable, protein and lipid rich structures have a refractive index of around 1.45. So the game is to adjust the refractive index of the water around it towards 1.45, which would make it more transparent.

Whatever we do to the water, we also need to make sure that we don't make the absorbance property too high. If κ gets too high, then we'd end up absorbing all the light and it won't go transparent.

So how do we shift the refractive index? To understand refractive indices, we first need to understand polarisation. To first order, a material consists of electrons bound to nuclei. When an electric field is applied to a material, the relative positions of the electrons to their nuclei change.

from [http://hyperphysics.phy-astr.gsu.edu/hbase/electric/dielec.html#c1]

For a positively charged particle and a negatively charged particle, polarisation is the magnitude of that charge multiplied by the displacement of one from the other. To calculate the polarisation, we need to model how far electrons displace from the nucleus under the electric field.

Electric fields provide a force on charges that are free. To model the effect of an electric field on a material, we treat the positive nucleus as fixed, and the electrons as free. To calculate the effect of the system, we'll use the Lorentz oscillator model.

In this model, the electrons are modelled to be bound to the nucleus like a damped spring, with the electric field applying a forcing. We can solve it exactly how we would solve a damped spring problem:

Newton's second law for the electron, with the light's field oscillating at ω:

\(m\ddot{x} = -m\omega_0^2\, x \;-\; m\gamma\,\dot{x} \;-\; e\,E_0\, e^{-i\omega t}\)

If we try an Ansatz for the position of the electron x(t) = x₀ e^(−iωt) (the electron oscillates at the driving frequency), we get that the position of the electron relative to the nucleus is given by the following expression.

\(x(t) = \frac{-e/m}{\omega_0^2 - \omega^2 - i\gamma\omega}\; E(t)\)

The dipole moment is p = −ex, and with N electrons per unit volume the polarisation per unit volume is

\(\mathbf{P} = N p = \frac{N e^2/m}{\omega_0^2 - \omega^2 - i\gamma\omega}\; \mathbf{E}\)

In this setup, ω₀ represents the natural frequency of the bound electron, which is the frequency the molecule absorbs at (for tartrazine, the 425 nm peak), γ represents the damping rate, which sets how broad that absorption peak is, and ω is the frequency of the electric field. Now we've found polarisation, we want to relate it to the refractive index itself. To do that, we need to do some gymnastics with two identities.

By convention, the polarisation can be written as proportional to the electric field

\(\mathbf{P} = \varepsilon_0\,\chi\,\mathbf{E}\)

where ε₀ is the permittivity of free space, χ is the electric susceptibility (a dimensionless number that says how easily the material polarises), and E is the electric field. Comparing with the Lorentz oscillator result above,

\(\chi(\omega) = \frac{N e^2/(\varepsilon_0 m)}{\omega_0^2 - \omega^2 - i\gamma\omega}\)

To relate our polarisation, and electric susceptibility to the refractive index, we use the following trick. The below is an AI-assisted proof with manual checking.

This degree of polarisation and the electric field is encoded in something called the electric displacement field D. And the relationship between D and the electric field is linear, with the coefficient called the relative permittivity, εᵣ. P here represents the polarisation per unit volume, and is the average induced dipole moment across all of the material.

\(\mathbf{D} = \varepsilon_0 \varepsilon_r \mathbf{E} = \varepsilon_0 \mathbf{E} + \mathbf{P}\)

It turns out that the relative permittivity is related to the complex refractive index as follows:

\(n_c^2 = (n' + i\kappa)^2 = \varepsilon_r\)

The proof of the relationship between refractive index and permittivity for a standard electric wave is standard, and is in the footnote below.² And so, to change the complex refractive index, we need to change the relative permittivity of the material.

To proceed, we use an approximation. The electric displacement field is a function of the polarisation of a material. But when we mix two materials together, we can add their polarisation densities.

Before adding tartrazine, we have that water obeys

\(\mathbf{D} = \varepsilon_0\,\varepsilon_{r,\mathrm{water}}\,\mathbf{E} = \varepsilon_0\mathbf{E} + \mathbf{P}_{\mathrm{water}}\)

Then when we add the dye, we get

\(\mathbf{D} = \varepsilon_0\mathbf{E} + \mathbf{P}_{\mathrm{water}} + \mathbf{P}_{\mathrm{tartrazine}}\)

But we know that each polarisation is proportional to the field, with its own susceptibility: P(water) = ε₀ χ(water) E and P(tartrazine) = ε₀ χ(dye) E, where χ(dye). Substituting that in, we get

\(\mathbf{D} = \varepsilon_0\left(1 + \chi_w + \chi_d\right)\mathbf{E}\)

Comparing with D = ε₀εᵣE, and using that water alone has εᵣ(water) = 1 + χ(water) = n(water)², the relative permittivity of the dyed water is

\(\varepsilon_r = \varepsilon_{r,\mathrm{water}} + \chi_d = n_w^2 + \chi_d\)

For a dilute dye, χ(dye) is small compared to n(water)², so we can expand the square root and use a Taylor expansion to get the modified refractive index of the water with the dye.

\(n_c = \sqrt{n_w^2 + \chi_d} = n_w\sqrt{1 + \frac{\chi_d}{n_w^2}} \;\approx\; n_w + \frac{\chi_d}{2 n_w}\)

n_c is complex. If we write it out as n_c = n′ + iκ and split the electric susceptibility of χ(dye) that we got into real and imaginary parts, the dye shifts the real refractive index and introduces absorption by

\(\Delta n' = n' - n_w = \frac{\mathrm{Re}\,\chi_d}{2 n_w}, \qquad \kappa = \frac{\mathrm{Im}\,\chi_d}{2 n_w}\)

And putting in the Lorentz form of χ(dye) that we got earlier

\(\Delta n' = \frac{N e^2}{2 n_w \varepsilon_0 m}\,\frac{\omega_0^2 - \omega^2}{(\omega_0^2 - \omega^2)^2 + \gamma^2\omega^2}, \qquad \kappa = \frac{N e^2}{2 n_w \varepsilon_0 m}\,\frac{\gamma\omega}{(\omega_0^2 - \omega^2)^2 + \gamma^2\omega^2}\)

For tartrazine and red light, ω is below the resonance ω₀, so ω₀² − ω² > 0 and Δn′ is positive. This means the dye raises the refractive index of the water. Meanwhile κ carries a factor of γω in the numerator and is only large near ω ≈ ω₀,, which means that we don't get absorbance.

References

Ou Z, Duh YS, Rommelfanger NJ, Keck CHC, Jiang S, Brinson K Jr, Zhao S, Schmidt EL, Wu X, Yang F, Cai B, Cui H, Qi W, Wu S, Tantry A, Roth R, Ding J, Chen X, Kaltschmidt JA, Brongersma ML, Hong G. Achieving optical transparency in live animals with absorbing molecules. Science. 2024 Sep 6;385(6713):eadm6869. doi: 10.1126/science.adm6869. Epub 2024 Sep 6. PMID: 39236186; PMCID: PMC11931656.

² Here are Maxwell's equations for electric and magnetic fields in a material. This is generated by Claude.

\(\nabla \cdot \mathbf{D} = \rho_f, \qquad \nabla \cdot \mathbf{B} = 0, \qquad \nabla \times \mathbf{E} = -\frac{\partial \mathbf{B}}{\partial t}, \qquad \nabla \times \mathbf{H} = \mathbf{J}_f + \frac{\partial \mathbf{D}}{\partial t}\)

\(\mathbf{D} = \varepsilon_0 \mathbf{E} + \mathbf{P} = \varepsilon_0 \varepsilon_r \mathbf{E}, \qquad \mathbf{B} = \mu_0 \mathbf{H} \quad \text{(non-magnetic)}\)

The question is then - how do any of these relate to the refractive index?

No free charges or currents (ρ = 0, J = 0), non-magnetic. Faraday's law says that the curl of an electric field is the negative of the magnetic field's time derivative. Take the curl of Faraday's law, and then substitute in

\(\nabla \times (\nabla \times \mathbf{E}) = -\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\,\nabla \times \mathbf{B}\)

Ampère–Maxwell with J = 0:

\(\nabla \times \mathbf{H} = \frac{\partial \mathbf{D}}{\partial t}\)

Substitute B = μ₀H and D = ε₀E + P = ε₀εᵣE:

\(\nabla \times \mathbf{B} = \mu_0 \frac{\partial \mathbf{D}}{\partial t} = \mu_0 \varepsilon_0 \frac{\partial \mathbf{E}}{\partial t} + \mu_0 \frac{\partial \mathbf{P}}{\partial t} = \mu_0 \varepsilon_0 \varepsilon_r \frac{\partial \mathbf{E}}{\partial t}\)

This is where εᵣ enters: the polarisation current ∂P/∂t adds to the vacuum displacement current. Then (taking εᵣ constant in time, i.e. working at a single frequency)

\(\nabla \times (\nabla \times \mathbf{E}) = -\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\,\nabla \times \mathbf{B} = -\mu_0 \varepsilon_0 \varepsilon_r \frac{\partial^2 \mathbf{E}}{\partial t^2}\)

\(\nabla \times (\nabla \times \mathbf{E}) = \nabla(\nabla \cdot \mathbf{E}) - \nabla^2 \mathbf{E} = -\nabla^2 \mathbf{E}\)

Then if we equate both sides, we get a plane wave equation

\(\Rightarrow \quad \nabla^2 \mathbf{E} = \frac{\varepsilon_r}{c^2}\frac{\partial^2 \mathbf{E}}{\partial t^2}, \qquad c^2 = \frac{1}{\mu_0 \varepsilon_0}\)

Plane wave E = E₀ e^(i(kz − ωt))

\(k^2 = \varepsilon_r \frac{\omega^2}{c^2}\)

Comparing with k = (n′ + iκ) ω/c from the attenuating wave written earlier,

\(\varepsilon_r(\omega) = n_c(\omega)^2 = (n' + i\kappa)^2 = n'^2 - \kappa^2 + 2 i n' \kappa\)

You can see the locations of known outdoor surveillance cameras in the app.

Matthew G Eddy/Shutterstock

MapQuest has been on quite the unexpected tear over the last couple of months. The mapping service's app surged in popularity after it refused to refer to Lake Ontario as Lake America (unlike Google Maps and Apple Maps). MapQuest also added useful, long-overdue features like Android Auto support and public transit directions.

The app now has another handy tool. You can toggle a layer that shows known outdoor surveillance cameras and license plate readers.

The layer will show you where Flock cameras are. It also displays the locations of cameras from the likes of Motorola Solutions (Vigilant), Genetec, Axis Communications, Axon, Leonardo (ELSAG), Neology, Rekor, PlateSmart, Ubicquia and Verkada. The layer sits alongside options to view traffic and incidents, so it should be easy to find in the app.

MapQuest announced the update with a short video that's set to Rockwell's "Somebody's Watching Me." Chef's kiss, no notes.

You might not be able to easily avoid these cameras on your commute or other usual routes, but the layer may be helpful in illustrating how pervasive these things are in your area. It's useful information to have for those who are trying to rid their neighborhoods of surveillance cams.

item.title: Israeli settlers attack olive framers & Washington Post journalist in West Bank (127 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/oct/16/israeli-settlers-attack-olive-farmers-west-bank-washington-post-journalist-heidi-levine, See on Hacker News

Israeli settlers have attacked Palestinians across the occupied West Bank in a coordinated movement to disrupt the annual olive harvest, burning cars and trees and injuring Palestinians and a Washington Post photographer.

Masked settlers wielding clubs and other weapons attacked people attempting to harvest their olives in West Bank towns on Friday. Palestinian authorities said they recorded attacks in eight villages, and injuries among at least 20 people.

It was the latest series of attacks in a deadly campaign of Israeli settler violence against Palestinians in recent months, violence which has drawn accusations of “ethnic cleansing”, including from the British government.

In the town of Abu Falah, near Ramallah, at least 80 settlers, some of whom were carrying firearms or clubs, gathered to stop Palestinians from harvesting their olives, using slingshots to hurl rocks at the farmers in view of Israeli military vehicles. When some of the Palestinians then picked up rocks to defend themselves, the Israeli military fired teargas in their direction.

The Israeli Foreign Press Association said in a statement: “This is the latest in a long line of violent attacks by Israeli settlers against journalists and other civilians in the occupied West Bank. Yet our repeated calls for action to confront this lawlessness have been ignored by Israeli authorities.”

Among those injured was the Washington Post photographer Heidi Levine, who was beaten by settlers in an attack that lasted more than 10 minutes, according to witnesses. Settlers stole her passport, phone, wallet and equipment.

“I was attacked, pushed to the ground. Luckily, I had my flak jacket and helmet, otherwise I probably wouldn’t even be here, because they just kept kicking and kicking me,” Levine said from a hospital bed in Ramallah. She said the attack ended when her Palestinian colleagues intervened to save her.

In a statement, the Washington Post said Levine had been wearing visible markings clearly identifying her as a journalist.

The office of Israel’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, said that the facts surrounding the attack on Levine were “unclear”, suggesting the attack was the fault of “200 Arabs and far-left activists” who confronted Israeli youths. The office added that it condemned “violence against anyone”.

There has been a surge of settler violence against Palestinians over the past month. Settlers have carried out at least 170 attacks since 27 September, around the start of the annual olive harvest, according to Yesh Din, an Israeli rights group.

Every year, settlers attack Palestinians trying to harvest their olives, but there has been a rise in violence this year as Israel’s elections approach at the end of October.

At least four Palestinians had been killed and more than 100 others injured over the past month, Palestinian authorities said. Thousands of trees have been damaged.

Israel imposed new rules on the olive harvest this year, barring Palestinians from harvesting their trees located in Area C, an area under the Israeli military’s control, which comprises most of the West Bank’s agricultural land.

The new orders prohibit Palestinians from entering about 8,800 hectares (21,800 acres) of agricultural land – a 30% increase from the year prior – without the approval of the Israeli military. By contrast, the military gave Israeli citizens access to more land this year.

The rights group Peace Now says the military decreased the amount of land Israeli citizens were prohibited, for the purpose of preventing settler violence, from entering from about 1,070 hectares in 2025 to 680 hectares in 2026.

The olive harvest is an economic lifeline for Palestinians and has grown in importance since Israel revoked work permits for many Palestinians in the West Bank after the Hamas-led attack on 7 October 2023.

Photos and videos showed large swathes of agricultural land with uprooted olive trees in Kufur Malek, outside Ramallah, where Israeli bulldozers razed trees.

Settlers rarely face accountability for their violence, even when well-documented. Rights groups say settlers enjoy the protection of the Israeli military, which intervenes only if Palestinians try to defend themselves.

Netanyahu, has on occasion condemned the violence, which he says is due to just about 100 settlers, but he has taken few steps to stop it.

Settlements have rapidly expanded across the West Bank under his rightwing government, leading to international condemnation. The UN and most countries judge settlements to be in violation of international law.

Friday’s attack in Abu Falah followed a similar attack hours earlier near the West Bank village of Turmus Ayya, where settlers burned three cars after attacking Palestinians harvesting olives.

Videos shared by the Israeli rights group B’tselem showed hundreds of bags of olives “violently” stolen by Israeli settlers from Palestinians and taken to Israeli olive presses.

Sarit Michaeli, an independent activist, said settlers were stealing Palestinians’ olive crop on a scale “never seen before in my 22-year history of working on this issue”.

A spokesperson for the US embassy in Jerusalem said it was aware of reports of the attack and declined to comment further due to privacy laws.

item.title: FLUX 3 Image Klein (204 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://bfl.ai/blog/flux-3-image-klein, See on Hacker News

Today we are releasing FLUX 3 Image Klein, a 5.6B parameter open weights model for text-to-image generation, image editing and multi-reference generation with up to 10 reference images. It shares core capabilities with the full FLUX 3 Image model: native 4K generation, pixel-perfect editing, and bounding boxes that control where elements are placed or confine edits to a defined area.

FLUX 3 Image Klein builds on FLUX 3's shared learnings across images, video and audio. Images contribute spatial detail, video adds motion and physical dynamics, and audio provides information about events and interactions. Together, these signals help the model generate images that feel grounded in the real world.

The release includes a base model for fine-tuning and a step distilled model for low-latency generation, along with FP8, INT8 and NVFP4 builds developed with NVIDIA support, under the FLUX Kommunity License.

Try it in the BFL API · Download the weights

Leading open weights quality with fewer parameters

In internal evaluations, FLUX 3 Image Klein ranks first in text-to-image, multi-reference generation and image editing, ahead of larger open weights models. It also rates above the closed models in the comparison, Ideogram V4.5 and FLUX.2 [pro]. At 5.6B parameters, it is the smallest open model in the comparison, against 7B for Qwen-Image 2.1 and 12.9B for Krea 2. Compared with FLUX.2 [klein] 9B, it gains 91 Elo in text-to-image and 70 in image editing, with 38% fewer parameters.

FLUX 3 Image Klein was also optimized for consumer GPUs. Fewer parameters make it practical to run locally and cheaper to adapt, and teams with data sovereignty or local deployment requirements can evaluate and adapt the model on their own infrastructure. This is also key for on-device image editing, allowing consumers to edit images directly on their favorite laptops. The generator weights require 11.2 GB in BF16 and 5.6 GB in FP8. With the INT8 build, FLUX 3 Image Klein runs on NVIDIA GeForce RTX GPUs with as little as 8GB of VRAM, through ComfyUI or Diffusers, extending what FLUX.2 [klein] started to even smaller hardware. With the distilled model and the INT8 build, it generates a 1MP image in about 4 seconds on an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5090 and under 9 seconds on an RTX 4070 through ComfyUI.

The base checkpoint is built for fine-tuning: Diffusers and Ostris's AI Toolkit support LoRA training from day one, and NVIDIA's NeMo AutoModel ships recipes that work directly from the released checkpoints.

For even faster production workloads that need lower latency, we also work with teams on specific customizations that get you there. Get in touch.

On the speed–quality frontier

FLUX 3 Image Klein also extends the speed–quality Pareto frontier. Through the BFL API, it delivers lower latency than Qwen-Image 2.1, FLUX.2 [pro], Ideogram V4.5 and Krea 2, and the highest rating at its latency and above. In the charts below, the violet line traces the highest rating available at each latency and the gray line shows the previous frontier.

Latency is measured end to end, from request submission to the finished 1 MP image, including queueing. FLUX 3 Image Klein was timed on our servers. Other models were timed from the client, which includes polling and network time. Krea 2 was timed on its Medium tier; its Large tier took 31.1 seconds for text-to-image.

Get started

FLUX 3 Image Klein is available today as open weights and through the BFL API.

Try it

  • BFL API: the distilled model is available as flux-3-image-klein, with prompt upsampling and pixel restoration, which preserves unedited regions of an image exactly. Pricing starts at $0.009 per 1K image.
  • Playground or Hugging Face.

Build with it

  • Weights on Hugging Face: base and distilled.
  • Reference inference code, including a Gradio demo for bounding-box control.
  • Try it out on Hugging Face Spaces.
  • Day-one support in ComfyUI, Hugging Face Diffusers, TensorRT-LLM, SGLang Diffusion and vLLM-Omni.
  • LoRA training with Ostris's AI Toolkit and recipes in NVIDIA NeMo AutoModel.
  • Trained on NVIDIA GB200 NVL72 and optimized for NVIDIA's accelerated computing platform, serving through NVIDIA TensorRT LLM, vLLM-Omni and SGLang Diffusion.
  • On NVIDIA GB300, the distilled model generates a 1MP image in under 0.6 seconds in NVFP4. Serving a LoRA adds around 5% to generation time.

License

The weights are available under the FLUX Kommunity License, which allows free commercial use for individuals and companies with annual revenue under $5M, alongside research and non-commercial use. Larger organizations can deploy commercially through our self-hosted licensing options or API.

Safety

In an effort to make AI technology both open and safe, we implement multiple safeguards throughout the model development lifecycle to combat misuse. These include dataset filters during pre-training to limit exposure to harmful content, and targeted fine-tuning during post-training to suppress harmful behaviors, making it progressively harder to elicit harmful content. Ahead of the release, the FLUX 3 Image Klein checkpoints were rigorously red teamed internally and evaluated by our external safety partner Cinder, demonstrating substantially fewer vulnerabilities than other popular open weights models. More on our safety methodology is available here.

FLUX 3 Image Klein is the second open weights release from the FLUX 3 family, following FLUX 3 Action. More will follow.

Learn more

  • FLUX 3: Real World Models, the research behind the FLUX 3 family
  • FLUX 3 Action, our open weights 7B model for robot control
